iconic_games.note: Hosted the opening match of the expanded 32-team 2025 FIFA Club World Cup on its natural-grass surface; Al Ahly 0-0 Inter Miami, 14 June 2025, attendance 65,326. Additional group-stage fixtures also staged here.

iconic_games_note: Hard Rock Stadium has a genuine top-flight football history (unlike pure-NFL bowls): it hosted the 2024 Copa America Final (Argentina 1-0 Colombia, a.e.t.) and 2025 FIFA Club World Cup group matches (incl. the Al Ahly 0-0 Inter Miami opener) on natural grass. It is also a major non-football venue, having hosted six Super Bowls (XXIII 1989, XXIX 1995, XXXIII 1999, XLI 2007, XLIV 2010, LIV 2020 — NON-association-football / American-football events) and multiple college football national championships (NON-association-football).

renovations.change: Natural-grass (Tifway 419 Bermuda) playing surface for the World Cup; FIFA mandates natural grass and the venue already uses Bermuda, so grass was laid/regrown for the tournament. Installation video drew online skepticism but the venue had already staged the 2024 Copa America and 2025 Club World Cup on real grass.

city_history.founded: 2003 (city of Miami Gardens incorporated 2003; Hard Rock Stadium opened 1987; within Greater Miami metro)
city_history.significance: Miami Gardens is a city in Miami-Dade County, Florida, incorporated in 2003, and the home of Hard Rock Stadium (opened 1987); it sits within the Greater Miami metropolitan area, a major US gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean.
city_history.football_culture: Football culture hangs on the Greater Miami metro rather than the suburban locality of Miami Gardens: Miami is one of the most football-passionate US markets, driven by its large Latin American and Caribbean diaspora. It is home to Inter Miami CF (Lionel Messi's club since 2023) and routinely hosts blockbuster internationals and tournaments — the 2024 Copa America Final and 2025 FIFA Club World Cup matches both at Hard Rock Stadium.

sources.title: Copa America 2024: Argentina wins Miami final — CNN

stadium_history_facts: Opened August 16, 1987 (first preseason game); original name Joe Robbie Stadium (1987-1996), built at a construction cost of $115 million.

Cycled through many naming-rights names: Pro Player Park/Stadium (1996-2005), Dolphins/Dolphin Stadium (2005-2009), Land Shark Stadium (2009-2010), Sun Life Stadium (2010-2016), New Miami Stadium (2016), then Hard Rock Stadium (2016-present).

Home of the NFL's Miami Dolphins since 1987; former home of MLB's Florida/Miami Marlins (1993-2011, who won the 1997 and 2003 World Series here); hosts the Miami Hurricanes (NCAA football, since 2008) and the Miami Open tennis tournament (since 2019).

2015-2016 renovation: privately funded by owner Stephen Ross; added corner video boards, additional suites, and an open-air canopy (anchored by four corner spires) covering most of the seating bowl; capacity reduced from the original ~75,000 to ~65,000 (64,767). Wikipedia (oldid 1360727139) states $350 million; some news sources state ~$500 million (contested).
Hosted six Super Bowls (XXIII, XXIX, XXXIII, XLI, XLIV, LIV) and multiple college football national-championship games.

Hosted the 2024 Copa America Final and 2025 FIFA Club World Cup matches (incl. the Al Ahly 0-0 Inter Miami opener); temporarily renamed 'Miami Stadium' for the 2026 FIFA World Cup under FIFA's clean-venue naming policy.
For the 2026 World Cup it hosts seven matches: four group-stage games, one Round of 32, one quarter-final, and the third-place (Bronze) match on July 18, 2026.
